newsitem.title: JAPAN: Banks may write off NCB units' loans early - sources.
newsitem.headline: Banks may write off NCB units' loans early - sources.

text.p: Several Japanese trust and commercial banks that extended loans to three failed non-bank financial affiliates of Nippon Credit Bank Ltd are considering writing off their loan losses in the year ended on March 31, banking sources said on Friday.
If they do so, the banks will revise their earnings forecasts for fiscal 1996/97, the sources said. They are expected to announce their actual results in May.
Japan's three long-term credit banks have a total of 422.6 billion yen worth of outstanding loans to the affiliates.
Trust banks have loans to the affiliates totalling 415.5 billion yen, while top commercial banks have loans worth 372.0 billion yen.
Agricultural cooperatives' loans to the affiliates total 232.7 billion yen and those of regional banks total 173.0 billion yen.
The institutions would forfeit a tax deduction by writing off the loan losses in 1996/97, but several banks are eager to dispose of their bad loans quickly, the sources said.
Loan losses are tax deductable under Japan's corporate tax system if they are written off in the same business year that the company receiving the loan became insolvent.
The Nippon Credit Bank (NCB) affiliates filed for bankruptcy on April 1, the first day of fiscal 1997/98, so creditors writing off loan losses in 1996/97 would lose the tax break.

Japanese banks are eager to speed up the disposal of their bad loans, however, as Japan will introduce new capital adequacy standards, under the so-called prompt corrective action (PCA) system, in April 1998, banking sources said.

"We are consulting with our certified accountant on whether or not we can write off the losses in the year ended in March," Mitsubishi Trust & Banking Corp's president Toyoshi Nakano said at a news conference earlier this week.
Sumitomo Bank Ltd, however, said on Thursday that it would not write off losses from the loans in 1996/97.
NCB said on Tuesday that three of its non-bank financial affiliates filed for bankruptcy at the Tokyo District Court earlier that day.
Although it did not give details on the scale of their debts, private credit research firm Teikoku Data Bank said on Tuesday that the affiliates' debts totalled 2.025 trillion yen.
